title: Near-stasis, checked against today's data
question: Does Mesozoic non-marine tetrapod diversity still show near-stasis in today's PBDB?

issues.text: 13 to 18 bins is a small sample, and neighbouring bins share long-ranging genera.
issues.fix: Read the slope with its interval, not only the verdict.

issues.text: The paper subsampled species within continental regions; this board subsamples genera worldwide, by occurrence.
issues.fix: Compare the size of the slopes, not the digits; a regional SQS is the closer check.

issues.text: The PBDB has grown since 2015, unevenly: the latest Cretaceous of North America most of all.
issues.fix: Look at the per-bin table: occurrences and coverage.

alternatives.question: Does the trend survive subsampling within one continent (North America) instead of worldwide?
alternatives.why: Drills down: the paper's regional design (Fig 5), with PBDB's cc=NOA.

alternatives.question: Do dinosaurs alone show the same near-stasis (the paper's Fig 5D)?
alternatives.why: Drills down into one clade: base_name=Dinosauria^Aves.

alternatives.question: Is the 4-fold jump after the K/Pg boundary still there in today's data?
alternatives.why: Expands past the Mesozoic: the Paleocene bin is on the board already.

hypotheses.statement: After subsampling, ln(genera) rises by less than 0.00581 per Myr across the Mesozoic.
hypotheses.null: The subsampled slope is 0.00581 per Myr or more.

hypotheses.statement: At face value, ln(genera found) doesn't change with time across all Mesozoic bins.
hypotheses.null: Face-value genus counts rise or fall with time.

method.summary: Bayesian linear regression of ln(genera) per bin on time (Myr), against the paper's upper bound (h1) and against zero (h2).

steps.title: Genera per bin (PBDB diversity) and subsampled genera (SQS) on the claim table
The slope of ln(genera) on time, per hypothesis
Near-stasis holds if the subsampled slope stays under the paper's bound

caveats: Only bins with coverage u ≥ 0.6 and 100 or more occurrences go in (13 of 18 today): the others' subsampled counts are close to their raw counts.
PBDB's bins and its terrestrial filter approximate the paper's bins and its list of excluded taxa.
A slope on ln(count) is the net diversification rate only if the bins' counts are comparable: subsampling is what tries to make them so.
